Amy: Now, Vanessa. Let's look at your wheel. The wheel has eight categories: physical environment, family health, personal growth, life planning, fun, work, social life. You give each a score from one to ten with ten being the highest. In each category Vanessa, you are under four. Can you explain that?
Vanessa: If you had asked me a month ago to do this chart, we wouldn't be discussing these low scores. I would get 9's if I did it then.
Amy: So what has changed?
Vanessa: After Sally left, I haven't really felt like myself. While she was here, we were really close friends. In fact, we had been best friends until the day she left.

Amy: You haven't talked about it with anyone? If you talked about it more, you would probably feel better.
Vanessa: Before coming here today, I had talked to Peter and Sally a little bit, but I mostly have just bottled things up. I guess when Sally was here, I always kind of knew she was going to leave one day. She has money and she has a wandering spirit. But it was the way she just suddenly disappeared.
Amy: Would you have felt differently today, if she had explained things in more detail?
Vanessa: Yeah. If I had talked to Sally more before she left, I would probably have felt better about her leaving.

Amy: What about Peter?
Vanessa: He's a good friend, I like Peter's goofy boyish charms, but sometimes he wears me out. Besides that, I think he is seeing someone now.
Amy: I see. Vanessa, in my opinion, because you are saddened by the loss of a friend you have taken all of your energy and focused it on work. The trouble is now, work no longer gives you the nutrients you need. If you created more of a balance, you would have more energy to counter this sadness. You'll find it gets easier as you get more balance in your life. But you are way out of balance and this is an obstacle.
Vanessa: Oh, you're good.

The Unreal Past: Hypothetical or Impossible?
You can use the second and third conditionals to talk about unreal events in the present, future and past.

You use the second conditional to talk about situations that are unreal in the present. It is also for things that are unlikely to happen in the future. If you write the if-clause first, you need a comma after it.

Second Conditional Structure:
if + simple past, would + base form
would + base form…if + simple past
Compare the first and second conditional in the sentences below:

If I win the lottery, I will buy a new car. (1st conditional, the person believes buying a car is likely to happen if they win the lottery)
If I won the lottery, I would buy a new car. (2nd conditional, the person believes this is unlikely they will win the lottery)

Another way to use the second conditional is with the “be” verb in the structure “If I were you, I would…” This is used to give advice. With the “be” verb, the “were” form is used for all subjects.
If I/you/he/she/it/we/they were…

Maria: I fell down yesterday and hit my head. I've had a headache all day and my vision is blurry.
Diego: If I were you, I would go to the doctor. That sounds serious!

Speaking Note: The would is often contracted to ‘d in speaking.
                                 I won the lottery, I'd buy a new car.
You use the third conditional to talk about imagined situations in the past. Because you are imagining what could have happened, you need to remember what the real situation is.

Examples:
I didn't study for my exams and I didn't pass. (real situation)
If I had studied for my exams, I would have passed. (imagined past situation)

I went to New York last week and took many pictures. (real situation)
If I hadn't gone to New York last week, I wouldn't have taken many pictures. (imagined past situation)

Third Conditional Structure:
if + past perfect, would have + past participle
would have + past participle…if + past perfect
If you had asked me a month ago to do this chart, we wouldn't be discussing these low scores.
If you talked about it more, you would probably feel better.
Would you have felt differently today if she had explained things in more detail?
If I had talked to Sally more before she left, I would probably have felt better about her leaving.
If you created more of a balance, you would have more energy to counter this sadness.
Time Clauses: A Brief Review
You can use time clauses to show relationships in time between different events.

You use different conjunctions in a time clause to express different relationships. A time clause is a dependent clause and must be connected to a main clause to form a complete sentence. It can come before or after a main clause. It is followed by a comma if it comes first.

Simultaneous Actions:
as
when
while

You can use these words:
  • For actions that are in progress or in the background when another action happens. You usually use progressive tenses with these words.
    • My mother cooked dinner as I was doing my homework.

  • For two longer situations happening at the same time, you use while.
    • While I was brushing my teeth, my sister was putting on her makeup.

  • For something that happened at a particular time in the past, you use when.
    • When I was in high school, my parents gave me my first cellphone.

Consecutive Actions:
when
once
before
until

You use these words:
  • For an action happening right after another, you use when + simple past in the time clause and simple past in the main clause. The time clause action happens first and the main clause action happens second.
    • When I hit my little brother, he bit me.

  • For two short events that happen at almost the same time, use as.
    • It started to rain (just) as I arrived home. I was lucky because I hadn't had my umbrella with me.

  • For something that has to happen before something else can happen, you use once. This is usually followed by a perfect tense.
    • Once the cake has cooled, we can start frosting it.

  • Use before for an action that occurred before something else. This might have finished a long time before the first action.
    • I worked at a restaurant before I went to university.

  • Use until when the first action happens up to the time of the second action.
    • I lived with my parents until I got married.

  • Use after to emphasize the first action. .
    • After I graduated from university, I took a year off.
